title: Kerala's Shigella Outbreak Exposes Growing Threat of Drug-Resistant Infections
excerpt: With 226 cases and six deaths this year, Kerala's recurring shigellosis outbreaks mirror a global surge in antibiotic-resistant Shigella strains that health authorities are struggling to treat.
body:
• Kerala has recorded 226 shigellosis cases and six deaths in 2026, with outbreaks in Kozhikode, Wayanad, Thrissur, and Alappuzha districts — most fatalities are children under 10.
  • Antimicrobial resistance is complicating treatment, as drug-resistant Shigella strains are rising globally — the CDC reports extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Shigella jumped from 0% of US isolates in 2011 to 8.5% in 2023.
  • As few as 10 Shigella bacteria can cause infection, and the pathogen can survive for weeks in water, making outbreaks particularly dangerous during monsoon season.
  • No FDA-approved antibiotic exists for XDR shigellosis, leaving physicians with limited treatment options for the most severe resistant cases.

Kerala's Recurring Battle

Kerala is facing yet another wave of shigellosis cases, with the state recording 226 infections and six deaths since the start of 2026. June alone saw 150 cases and four fatalities, with outbreaks concentrated in Kozhikode, Wayanad, Thrissur, and Alappuzha districts, according to state Health Minister K. Muraleedharan.

Four of the six deaths occurred in children under 10, underscoring the disease's disproportionate impact on younger populations whose immune systems are less equipped to fight the infection. A one-year-old child was reported in critical condition at Kozhikode Medical College Hospital.

Shigellosis — bacillary dysentery caused by Shigella bacteria — spreads through contaminated food and water, poor hygiene, and direct contact with infected individuals. What makes Shigella particularly dangerous is its extraordinarily low infectious dose.

"Shigella is able to withstand the hostile acidic environment of the human stomach. Outside the human body, it can stay alive in water for weeks together."

— Dr. Rajeev Jayadevan, former President, Indian Medical Association (IMA) Cochin

The Antibiotic Resistance Challenge

What elevates Kerala's outbreaks from a local health concern to a story of global significance is the growing shadow of antimicrobial resistance. Dr. Jayadevan emphasized that effective treatment requires culturing the specific organism and identifying which antibiotics it remains sensitive to — a process that varies by region.

"The antibiotic that might work for an outbreak in Chennai may not work in Calicut [Kozhikode] for a similar outbreak, as there will be a regional variation," he told Happiest Health.

This challenge is not unique to India. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention highlighted growing concerns about drug-resistant Shigella strains in its April 2026 Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. The CDC's analysis of 16,788 Shigella isolates collected through PulseNet between 2011 and 2023 found that extensively drug-resistant (XDR) strains — resistant to five commonly used antibiotics including ampicillin, azithromycin, ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole — jumped from 0% of isolates during 2011-2015 to 8.5% in 2023.

A Global Public Health Threat

"Shigellosis is one of those intestinal infections that responds well to antibiotics, by and large," said Dr. William Schaffner, professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. "But now we have strains of Shigella that are labeled extensively drug resistant, which means we don't have an FDA-approved antimicrobial that can be used against them."

The CDC estimates approximately 450,000 Americans develop shigellosis each year. While most cases resolve with rest and hydration, severe infections with resistant strains face an alarming therapeutic gap. Oral carbapenems, pivmecillinam, and fosfomycin may be effective against some resistant strains, but none have been FDA-approved for treating shigellosis.

"For patients who do need treatment and have a resistant strain, oral antibiotics won't work," said Dr. Ali Rezaie, medical director of the GI motility program at Cedars-Sinai. "For severe infections, physicians may use carbapenems given intravenously, which are the most reliable option for severe XDR infections but require hospitalization."

Prevention and What's Next

With treatment options narrowing, prevention remains the primary weapon against Shigella. Public health authorities in Kerala have ramped up surveillance and containment measures across affected districts. Basic hygiene measures — thorough handwashing with soap, safe drinking water, proper food handling, and fly control — remain the most effective preventive strategies.

Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) and zinc supplementation are recommended for managing symptoms. Physicians stress against self-medication, as inappropriate antibiotic use can further drive resistance.

The convergence of India's monsoon-driven outbreaks and the global rise in drug-resistant Shigella strains signals a growing public health challenge. Experts are calling for stronger surveillance, routine antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and investment in developing new antibiotics targeting resistant Shigella — before the therapeutic arsenal runs dry entirely.
